title: Skincare for men: the basics that actually work
dek: Three products do most of the job. Here's the evidence-led starter routine — and the hype worth ignoring.
bottom_line: Morning: gentle cleanser (or just water), a plain moisturiser, then broad-spectrum SPF 30+ sunscreen — every day, cloudy days and indoors-by-a-window included.
Evening: gentle cleanser, moisturiser. Only once that's an automatic habit, add a low-strength retinoid 2–3 nights a week.
Change one thing at a time and give it 8–12 weeks before deciding whether it works.
Persistent or scarring acne, a new or changing mole, or anything painful → see a GP or dermatologist, not a forum.

sections.heading: The routine most people actually need
sections.body:
Skincare marketing sells complexity. The evidence doesn't. For the large majority of people, three steps — cleanse, moisturise, and protect from the sun — deliver almost all of the realistic benefit. Everything beyond that is optimisation, and optimisation only pays off once the basics are consistent.

Consistency beats potency. A simple routine you actually do every day outperforms an elaborate one you abandon in a fortnight.

tips.claim: A gentle cleanser once or twice a day is enough
tips.detail: Harsh foaming washes that leave skin feeling 'squeaky' strip the barrier and can drive more oil and irritation. A mild, fragrance-free cleanser is plenty; if your skin runs dry, plain water in the morning is fine.

tips.claim: Moisturiser is for every skin type, oily included
tips.detail: A basic moisturiser supports the skin barrier. Oily skin still benefits — a light gel or lotion won't 'clog' the way people fear. Boring and fragrance-free is the goal, not expensive.

sections.heading: Sunscreen: the single highest-return habit
sections.body:
If you do one thing, do this. Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen is the most evidence-backed step in any routine: it is the main lever on long-term skin ageing, uneven tone, and skin-cancer risk. Nothing else in skincare has this strength of evidence behind it.

The best sunscreen is the one you'll actually wear daily, so pick a texture you like. Most people apply far too little — aim for roughly a two-finger length across face and neck, and top it up if you're outdoors for hours.

tips.claim: Daily broad-spectrum SPF 30+ is the anti-ageing step that works
tips.detail: Regular sunscreen use measurably slows visible photoageing and lowers skin-cancer risk. This is about as close to settled as skincare science gets.
Under-application is the most common mistake — a thin smear gives a fraction of the labelled protection. Two-finger length for face and neck; reapply every couple of hours in strong sun.

sections.heading: Actives worth adding — carefully
sections.body:
Once the basics are automatic, a few 'actives' have real evidence behind them. Add them one at a time, start low and slow, and expect results over months, not days.

More is not better. Stacking several strong actives at once is the fastest route to a wrecked barrier — the red, flaky, stinging skin that sends people right back to square one.

tips.claim: A retinoid is the best-evidenced 'anti-ageing' active
tips.detail: Topical retinoids (retinol over the counter, tretinoin on prescription) improve fine lines, texture and acne over months. Start 2–3 nights a week, buffer with moisturiser, and always pair with daytime sunscreen.

tips.claim: Vitamin C and exfoliating acids help — modestly
tips.detail: A morning vitamin-C serum can support tone alongside sunscreen; leave-on AHA/BHA acids help texture and mild breakouts. Genuinely useful, not miraculous, and easy to overdo.

sections.caution: Retinoids should not be used in pregnancy, and strong actives can badly irritate if layered too fast. Introduce one active at a time. If your skin turns red, raw, or stinging, stop and let the barrier recover before restarting.

sections.heading: Hype to ignore
sections.body: A lot of what's marketed to men — and pushed hard in looksmaxxing spaces — has little behind it. Spending here is mostly wasted money, and occasionally wasted skin.

tips.detail: Past cleanse–moisturise–protect (plus maybe one active), extra steps add cost and irritation risk, not results.

tips.claim: 'Pore-minimising' and 'detox' products don't do what they claim
tips.detail: Pore size is mostly genetic and can't be shrunk by a cleanser; skin doesn't 'detox' through a mask. These are marketing terms, not mechanisms.

tips.claim: Collagen drinks and most beauty supplements won't fix your face
tips.detail: Evidence for ingestible-beauty products is weak and often industry-funded. That money is better spent on sunscreen and sleep.

sections.heading: When to stop DIY-ing and see a professional
sections.body:
Skincare has a ceiling, and some things need a clinician. Recognising that line is harm reduction, not defeat.

Forums and creators are not a substitute for a diagnosis. Prescription treatments for acne, rosacea, or persistent pigmentation are more effective than anything on a shop shelf, and a professional manages them safely.

tips.claim: See a GP or dermatologist for persistent or severe acne
tips.detail: Moderate-to-severe or scarring acne has effective prescription treatments. Getting on them early prevents permanent scarring — don't just wait it out.

tips.claim: Get any new, changing, or unusual mole checked
tips.detail: Changes in size, shape or colour, or a spot that itches or bleeds, warrant a professional look. This is the one item on this page that can be genuinely serious.

sections.caution: This guide is general information, not medical advice. For diagnosis or treatment see a qualified professional — especially for anything painful, rapidly changing, or affecting your wellbeing.
